content_voiceover: Let's look at two classic parentage puzzles that hinge on the Bombay and Para Bombay phenomenon. First case: two O type parents produce a child who types as B. Second case: an O type father and an A type mother apparently produce an AB type daughter, which triggered a real Taiwanese court case where the husband accused his wife of infidelity. Both scenarios are explained by a rare mutation in the H gene, not the ABO gene. Remember, the H gene builds the precursor H antigen that A and B transferases then modify. If someone inherits two nonfunctional H alleles, they cannot express H antigen even if they carry functional A or B genes, so they type falsely as O on routine serology, a Para Bombay phenotype. In the court case, DNA confirmed paternity, and repeat testing showed the father was actually a hidden B subgroup or Para Bombay type. High yield pearl: in Bombay and Para Bombay individuals, you can detect the true hidden A or B antigen by testing saliva, since secretors express ABH antigens in body fluids independent of red cell expression.
keypoints: Bombay/Para-Bombay = defective H gene (hh), not ABO gene, causes false O typing
Explains seemingly impossible parent-child ABO combinations
Saliva testing reveals hidden A/B antigen via secretor status
Do not assume non-paternity from an ABO discrepancy alone
keypoint_voiceover: Remember, Bombay and Para Bombay phenotypes come from a defective H gene, not a defective ABO gene, so a person can carry functional A or B genes yet still type as O on routine serology. This explains seemingly impossible parent-child ABO combinations. The key testing trick: check saliva for A and B antigens, since secretor status reveals the hidden ABO genotype even when red cell typing looks like O.
